newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian poll results put pro-Abacha camp in lead.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian poll results put pro-Abacha camp in lead.

text.p: The political camp that supports Nigeria's military ruler, General Sani Abacha, took a strong early lead in the country's local elections, official results showed.
The military government cited peaceful voting on Saturday as proof of popular support for Abacha's controversial plan, criticised by the West, to transfer power to civilians next year.
Early results put the United Nigeria Congress Party (UNCP) in a commanding lead, followed by the Democratic Party of Nigeria (DPN). Three other legal parties were in the running.
Both the UNCP and DPN have declared their willingness to field Abacha as their candidate for promised presidential elections next year intended to end military rule.
In provisional official results declared for the Federal Capital Territory around Abuja, the UNCP swept all six local council chairmanships on offer plus 36 of 63 council seats.
In Lagos state, centred around Nigeria's largest city and commercial capital, the UNCP won eight of the 13 council chairmanships declared, state radio said.
The DPN took three and a third party, Grassroots Democratic Movement (GDN), two. A runoff will be held in seven local authorities where no clear winner emerged, the radio said.
The UNCP and DPN were neck and neck in northern Bauchi, winning six and five chairmanships respectively from the 14 declared. One went to the GDM while two go to a second round.
Exit polls forecast a similar trend nationwide for the poll to elect chairmen and councillors for 774 municipalities.
The trend appeared in line with the rating of the National Electoral Commission when it registered five political parties last September after the army lifted a ban on parties.

The commission said the UNCP had the widest national support, followed by the DPN. Both are centrist with their roots in the predominantly Islamic north, which has produced most of Nigeria's leaders since independence in 1960.
The results looked certain to fuel controversy on the future of Abacha, who seized power in 1993 after previous army rulers aborted a plan to return Nigeria to civil rule, sparking unrest.
He ignored pressure at home and from the West for an early return to democracy and pressed on with his own civil-rule plan. Saturday's poll was the first on party lines since 1993.
Pro-democracy activists say they believe Abacha will follow a growing band of military strongmen in West Africa who have legitimised their rule through carefully-controlled elections.

Abacha's only comment on the question of whether he will stand is that it depends on his "constituency." He has not stated if the constituency is the army or another group but supporters say he is as free as anyone to contest elections once he quits the army.
Many veteran politicians stayed on the sidelines of the local elections as their parties were not registered. They are expected to decide their affiliation after results are known.
Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro said the orderly and enthusiastic voting showed that Nigerians endorsed the government's programme to transfer power to civilians in 1998.
"We want to show the world that Nigeria is the father of democracy," he told reporters in the northern city of Kaduna.
Local observers and Western diplomats said they were surprised by the relaxed manner of the voting.
